title: Fewest Cuts Into Palindromes
statement:
You get a string s. Cut it into pieces so that every piece reads the same forwards and backwards. Return the smallest number of cuts that achieves this.

A single character is always a palindrome, so s.length − 1 cuts always work. If s is already a palindrome, the answer is 0.

examples.why: "a" | "baab". Grabbing the longest palindrome at the front first gives "aba" | "a" | "b", which needs 2 cuts.
The whole string is already a palindrome.
No two neighbouring letters match, so every letter is its own piece.

constraints: s has only lowercase English letters
hints: Think about the last piece. If it is s[j..i], how many cuts did the part before it need?
Let cuts[i] be the fewest cuts for the prefix of length i. Then cuts[i] = min over palindromic s[j..i−1] of cuts[j] + 1. Checking each palindrome directly makes this O(n³).
Find all palindromes cheaply: expand around each centre. Every palindrome s[l..r] you discover offers cuts[r + 1] = cuts[l] + 1.

explain.intuition:
Greedy fails: the longest palindrome at the front may split the rest badly. Instead look at the last piece. If the prefix of length i ends with the palindrome s[j..i−1], its cost is the best cost of the prefix of length j plus one cut. Taking the minimum over every such j gives an exact answer.

The slow part is knowing which substrings are palindromes. Expanding around every centre (each letter, and each gap between letters) visits every palindrome exactly once, and each one immediately offers a candidate for cuts[r + 1]. That is O(n²) time with only O(n) memory.
steps: Let cuts[i] be the fewest pieces minus one for s[0..i−1]. Start with cuts[i] = i − 1 (every letter alone), so cuts[0] = −1.
For each centre, expand l and r outward while s[l] === s[r]. Do this for odd centres (l = r = c) and even centres (l = c, r = c + 1).
For each palindrome s[l..r] found, set cuts[r + 1] = min(cuts[r + 1], cuts[l] + 1).
Process centres from left to right: cuts[l] only depends on palindromes ending before l, which come from earlier centres.
pitfalls: Cutting off the longest palindrome first. "abaab" shows it loses.
Counting pieces instead of cuts. The answer is one less than the number of pieces, which is why cuts[0] = −1.
Re-checking each substring for being a palindrome from scratch inside the DP. That is O(n³) and too slow for n = 2000.

solutions.title: DP with a direct palindrome check
solutions.idea: For each prefix end, try every last piece and test it character by character.

solutions.title: Palindrome table plus DP
solutions.idea: Fill a table pal[j][i] from shorter to longer ranges, then run the same DP with O(1) palindrome checks.

solutions.title: Expand around centres
solutions.idea: Visit every palindrome by growing it from its centre, and let each one improve the cut count right after it.

followups: Return the pieces themselves, not just the number of cuts.
List every way to cut the string into palindromes. Why does that need backtracking rather than this DP?
